about: Facts about Cavan County Council's winter service, taken from the documents listed in the sources. Each item names its source id. Where the council document is the 2023/24 edition, it may have changed since.

council_policy_and_practice.text: Cavan County Council will endeavour to carry out winter service operations to the best of its ability, within resources available, to alleviate problems caused by adverse weather conditions.

The council maintains over 3000 km of national, regional and local roads. It does not have the operational or financial resources to salt the whole network, so it has a schedule of priority routes salted each time it is deemed necessary.

National roads N3, N54, N55, N87, and N16 (salted by Leitrim County Council), plus the R198 to the hospital and the R935 salt depot. Level of service: treated during all weather events. When resources become limited, Priority 1 routes are treated to the exclusion of all others, and are treated and retreated ahead of all other routes.

Most regional roads and some key local primary roads: R188, R198, R154, R199, R203, R194, R191, R178, R935, R192, R162, R190, R201, R202, R205, R165, R164, R197, R200, R207, R206, R212, plus local roads L1045, LP1532, L2516, L2517, L3020, L3013, L3014, L3015, L3021, L3026, L3029, L2500, L2502. Treated as part of normal winter service but may have interruptions in certain severe weather events.

All other roads: local recognised hazard locations as directed by Municipal District Engineers. Not treated in normal winter service, but may receive intermittent treatment during certain severe weather events.

The Municipal Districts may carry out extra localised winter maintenance subject to resources and weather, at the discretion of the Municipal Engineers. The plan warns the council may no longer be able to assist local problem areas such as farms, schools and churches as it did in the past.

A roster of Duty Engineers monitors weather forecasts, uses the Met Eireann consultancy service, monitors road conditions in the Vaisala Manager system, and manages deployment with the Machinery Yard. All Priority 1 and 2 call-out decisions are made by the Duty Engineers.

TII road weather stations, the Vaisala Manager road weather system, and Met Eireann forecasts. In County Cavan Vaisala Manager records data from two weather and ice monitoring stations on the N3, at Virginia and Butlersbridge. Stations report road surface temperature, dew temperature, road wetness, wind and salt concentration. The plan says the forecasting system is accurate to about 85% at best, so there are a few days a winter when frost is not forecast but occurs, and local variations are hard to forecast.

Machinery Yard: 9 trucks, demountable salt spreaders (3 x 9 m3 brine, 2 x 9 m3 mounted brine, 1 x 6 m3 brine, 5 x 5 m3), 10 snow ploughs, 1 loading shovel, and a brine saturation station at Moynehall. Staff: 3 normal, 8 on call, managed centrally and normally assigned to roads areas. Municipal Districts: Cavan-Belturbet has 3 mini salters on crew cabs, a tractor with plough in West Cavan, and tractor spreaders in West Cavan and Cavan town; Ballyjamesduff has 2 mini spreaders for crew cabs; Bailieborough-Cootehill has 2 mini salters for crew cabs.

Capacity of about 2,750 tonnes, enough for about 30 pre-salting runs for the county in standard frost conditions. In severe snowfalls a contingency plan may provide grit at strategic locations in each Municipal District.

Number of times crews were called out to salt scheduled routes: 2007/08: 37; 2008/09: 66; 2009/10: 77; 2011/12: 52; 2012/13: 85; 2013/14: 77; 2014/15: 72; 2015/16: 58; 2016/17: 55; 2017/18: 100; 2018/19: 42; 2019/20: 61; 2020/21: 61; 2021/22: 46; 2022/23: 50. The table has no entry for 2010/11. The plan says the frequency depends on the severity of the winter.

A purchase-a-salt-bin scheme lets community groups, businesses, schools and churches buy a bin (EUR 170 with one fill, EUR 120 delivery only) to treat local roads and footpaths in severe prolonged cold. Introduced after the winters of 2009 and 2010.

About 90 tonnes of salt is used in a night's salting, covering about 500 km of the national and regional network. The council uses Ice Cast cold weather alerts. It says salt does not guarantee normal speeds, that sleet and snow are especially dangerous, and that frost after rain can undo any benefit of salting. Salting takes time and conditions can change during it.

Northern Sound 25/01/2022: a Municipal District Area Manager said 20% of the county's road network is salted and the council does not have the resources to extend it. Extension is possible during prolonged cold spells, with national roads prioritised.

Anglo Celt 12/12/2024: councillors asked for the winter maintenance route to be extended to schools, a nursing home and other vulnerable locations, and some wanted gritters to use their own discretion on when to treat. A councillor noted that if rain comes the work is undone, and the Cathaoirleach noted that salt can damage road surfacing.

Anglo Celt 01/02/2026: council officials said it is not physically possible to salt all routes, that the salting time frame is four to six hours, that 645 km is salted per night, that there is some discretion for local roads based on traffic data, and that adding one route means taking away from the maintenance plan. Priority routes include Local Link and Bus Eireann routes where they are on priority roads. The officials said they are at the limit of what can be done, and that it is not just funding but also time.

Anglo Celt 07/01/2010: during the long cold spell the council was gritting about 1,028 km of road per night at about EUR 20,000 a night, used up to 1,100 tonnes of salt from Christmas Eve to 3 January, and ran short of supplies; national routes, the busiest regional roads and some other areas were gritted as resources allowed.

Monaghan 2025/26: 8 gritters, about 610 km of Priority 1 and 2 roads, mobilisation 1 hour, treatment 2 hours for Priority 1 and 3 to 5 hours for Priority 2, 3,000 to 3,500 tonnes of salt storage for about 50 runs. Mayo 2025/26: about 1,400 km treated, 10% of regional roads and 95% of local roads not salted, Met Eireann can only guarantee about 80% forecast accuracy, and up to 4 hours to salt a route. Louth: about 460 km, 32% of its network, 6 primary routes and 6 gritting vehicles. Galway: about 623 km, 100% of national roads and 20% of regional roads.

how_winter_watch_works.text: Forecast air temperature and dew point are adjusted to each route's elevation. Road surface temperature is estimated, not measured, as air temperature minus up to 1.5 C of night-time cooling on clear calm nights. GO means estimated surface at or below 1 C while damp (rain, or air within 1.5 C of dew point). MARGINAL means cold but dry, or at or below 2 C and damp. Otherwise NO-GO.

A logistic-regression model trained on ERA5-Land ground temperature gives a second opinion. If it disagrees with the rules engine the route is marked REVIEW and the more cautious call is shown. It tends to treat cold nights as risky and puts little weight on dryness, so on a dry clear frost it says risky while the rules say marginal.

Confidence is the share of designated routes where the rules engine and model agree: HIGH at 75% or more, MEDIUM from 50% to 74%, LOW below 50%. It measures how much the two independent checks agree. It is not a probability that ice will form.

Truck plan: each road's deadline is its forecast ice onset minus 15 minutes. Roads are assigned to trucks, Priority 1 first. A truck chains roads in deadline order and a new truck is used only when a road cannot be added without finishing late or going past a 6 hour run. Treatment is assumed at 20 km/h including turning and reloads, driving between roads at 60 km/h on straight-line distance x 1.3, 30 minutes mobilisation, and the yard assumed to be in Cavan town. Trucks leave as late as possible so each road is finished just before ice. These are assumptions, not council data.

History: 7 winters (October 2018 to March 2025) of ERA5 reanalysis, run through the same rules engine on designated routes. This is modelled, not observed road conditions. Compared with the council's real call-outs for 2018/19 to 2022/23 the tool's count of nights with a GO route correlates at 0.87 but undercounts by about 15%, on only 5 winters.

limits_of_what_is_known: The exact location of the council's yard and the real crew rosters are not published, so truck timings are approximations.
No road weather station readings or thermal mapping data are used. Only two N3 stations are known to exist in the county.
Call-out numbers are the council's own count of salting call-outs, not the number of nights with ice.
Traffic volumes, collision history and school bus routes are not in the tool, so they cannot be used to compare routes.
The Cavan plan available is the 2023/24 edition. Newspaper reports from 2026 give slightly different figures (for example 645 km a night).
